title: 怎样写一条公道的差评
title_en: The Art of the Fair Review
summary_zh: 旅途中吃了一顿糟糕的饭，回来就打一星？作者认为写点评是现代旅行者的小小责任，并提出三条原则：对事不对人、讲分寸、写具体。适合学习议论文的立论、让步与举例。
body: Most of us have done it: returned from a disappointing dinner abroad, opened a review site and, still irritated, typed out a single furious line. It feels like justice at the time. In reality, a one-star rant tells future travellers almost nothing, and it can do lasting harm to a small family business that has no way of answering back. I would argue that writing reviews has become a minor civic duty of the modern traveller, and like any duty, it is worth doing well. The first principle is to separate a critique of the experience from a verdict on the people. "The waiter was rude" is an accusation; "we waited nearly an hour and nobody explained why" is information, and information is what readers can actually use. The second principle is proportion. A delicious meal served on a chipped plate is still a delicious meal, and a guesthouse that was perfectly comfortable should not be punished for failing to entertain you like a theme park. Equally, if the heating was inadequate in midwinter, say so plainly, but leave out the sarcasm. Reviewers who strive for fairness tend to be believed; those who rage are quietly ignored. Specificity is the third principle, and perhaps the most overlooked. A single concrete illustration — the cold soup, the broken lift, the owner who drove you to the station at dawn — does more than a paragraph of adjectives. Some platforms now invite users to nominate their favourite places for annual awards, and it is striking how often the winners are crowned not for luxury but for small acts of care that a reviewer bothered to describe. None of this means pretending, of course. A restaurant that has become a smash hit online may well deserve a cooler assessment from someone who simply ate there and paid the bill. Honesty and generosity, after all, are not opposites. The best reviews read like advice from a well-travelled friend: candid about what went wrong, precise about what went right, and written in the knowledge that a real person, somewhere, will read every word.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Travellers should stop posting negative reviews altogether
Reviews are most useful when they are fair, proportionate and specific
Review sites should remove all one-star ratings
Only professional critics should review restaurants and hotels

questions.prompt: Why does the writer contrast 'The waiter was rude' with a sentence about waiting nearly an hour?
options: To show that rude staff should be named in reviews
To show the difference between an accusation and useful information
To argue that slow service is the worst problem in restaurants
To suggest that longer reviews are always more helpful
questions.evidence: information is what readers can actually use

questions.prompt: What does "candid" mean in "candid about what went wrong"?
options: angry
secretive
polite but vague
honest and direct

questions.prompt: According to the writer, why does a one-star rant do harm?
options: It tells future travellers little and can hurt a small business that cannot reply
It is always deleted by the website
It is usually written by staff
It makes prices go up
questions.evidence: a one-star rant tells future travellers almost nothing

vocabulary.example: My friends' verdict was that the hotel was fine but far too expensive.
Her critique of the film was sharp but fair.
Try to keep a sense of proportion: one late train does not ruin a holiday.
I appreciated his candid advice about the job.
The lighting in the room was inadequate for reading.

expressions.note: lasting 强调影响持久；也可以说 do serious / real harm to sb/sth。
answer back 原指顶嘴，这里指被批评的一方没有机会解释，常用于讨论公平。
so 指代前面提到的情况；plainly 强调不绕弯、不阴阳怪气。
原指演出、电影、歌曲大获成功，现在也常形容走红的餐厅或产品。
议论文里用来防止读者误解、引出限定或让步，后接动名词或从句。
书面表达，后接完整句子，强调带着某种认识去做事。

knowledge.quote: A single concrete illustration — the cold soup, the broken lift, the owner who drove you to the station at dawn — does more than a paragraph of adjectives.
knowledge.explanation: 主语中心词是 A single concrete illustration（单数），破折号中间插入的三个例子不影响谓语，所以用 does。插入成分越长，越要找准中心词。

knowledge.quote: it is striking how often the winners are crowned not for luxury but for small acts of care
knowledge.explanation: it 是形式主语，真正的主语是 how often 引导的名词性从句，用陈述语序。It is striking how ... 是表达“令人惊讶的是……”的高级句型。

knowledge.quote: a guesthouse that was perfectly comfortable should not be punished for failing to entertain you like a theme park
knowledge.explanation: 介词 for 后接动名词 failing，be punished for doing 表示“因……而受罚”。fail 后面又接不定式 to entertain，动名词和不定式在这里自然连用。

speaking: 用 1 分钟口头“改写”一条你看过的差评：先说原句哪里不公道，再给出一个更具体、更有分寸的版本，用上 say so plainly。
writing: 用 200–250 词为一家你去过的餐厅或酒店写一条平衡的点评：至少一个具体细节、一个优点和一个缺点，语气坦率但不刻薄，用上 None of this means ...。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 ... who ... tend to ...; those who ... are ... 写一组对比，谈谈你观察到的两类人。
task.model: Reviewers who strive for fairness tend to be believed; those who rage are quietly ignored.

title: 冰川向导眼中的变化
title_en: Walking on Retreating Ice: A Glacier Guide on What Has Changed
summary_zh: 一位在同一条冰川上带了大半辈子徒步的向导，谈冰川退缩给工作带来的变化：更长的进山路、更难预测的危险、更严格的培训，以及她为什么仍然抱有希望。
body: Interviewer: You've been leading walks on this glacier for most of your working life. What has changed the most? Ingrid: The approach, more than anything. When I started, you stepped off the path almost straight onto the ice, whereas now there's a long walk across the bare rock and rubble that the glacier has left behind. We've even had to build a suspension bridge over a gorge that simply wasn't there before. Visitors often ask whether that's the warming they read about, and the honest answer is yes, although I'm a guide, not a scientist, so I try not to dress my impressions up as data. Interviewer: Does all this make the work more dangerous? Ingrid: It makes it less predictable, which in the mountains amounts to the same thing. Retreating ice behaves differently: crevasses open in places where there were none, and the rock above us loosens as it thaws. Interviewer: Is there a time of day you try to avoid? Ingrid: The afternoon, wherever possible. As the sun works on the ice, the meltwater streams swell, and you can get a sudden surge through a channel that was ankle-deep an hour earlier. The probability of rockfall rises in the heat too, so we start early and are usually off the ice by lunch. Interviewer: How do you prepare new guides? Ingrid: With an intensive season of training before they lead anyone alone: rope work, rescue, and above all reading the snow. Where fresh snow has been allowed to accumulate over a crevasse, it can form a bridge that looks solid and isn't. Every season seems to bring some new complication, so the training never stays the same for long. Interviewer: Do you ever feel you're guiding people to say goodbye? Ingrid: Some come with that idea, and I understand it. But I'd rather they left curious than mournful. If people see the ice with their own eyes, they tend to care about it in a way that no photograph manages. That, at least, keeps me hopeful.

questions.prompt: Which best describes Ingrid's attitude to the changes on the glacier?
options: She thinks visitors exaggerate them and pays them little attention
She adapts her work to them and still sees reasons for optimism
She believes guided walks on the glacier should now stop
She is mainly worried that fewer tourists will come
questions.evidence: That, at least, keeps me hopeful.

questions.prompt: Why does Ingrid's group usually leave the ice by lunch?
options: The suspension bridge is closed in the afternoon
Meltwater and falling rock become more of a risk as the day warms up
Visitors are too tired after the long walk in
New guides are only allowed to work in the morning
questions.evidence: The probability of rockfall rises in the heat too, so we start early and are usually off the ice by lunch.

questions.prompt: Why does Ingrid try "not to dress my impressions up as data"?
options: She has no time to collect measurements
She does not want to claim a scientific authority she lacks
She dislikes scientists
She does not believe the ice is melting
questions.evidence: I'm a guide, not a scientist

questions.prompt: What does "accumulate" mean in "allowed to accumulate over a crevasse"?
options: melt away
be cleared away
gradually build up
freeze solid
questions.evidence: Where fresh snow has been allowed to accumulate over a crevasse

vocabulary.example: After the storm, the mountain path was covered in rubble.
The guide roped us together because of the hidden crevasses.
The river freezes in winter and thaws in spring.
There was a sudden surge of water after the heavy rain.
Snow can accumulate quickly on the roof during a storm.

expressions.note: 回答“什么变化最大/最重要”时的口语开头，相当于 above all。

expressions.text: dress my impressions up as data
expressions.meaning: 把个人印象包装成数据
expressions.note: dress sth up as sth 指把某物装扮、包装成另一种样子，常暗示“不够真实”。
amount to 表示“等于、相当于”，常用来指出两件看似不同的事结果一样。
书面和口语都常用，放在句末表示“能做到就做到”。
强调亲身经历，常见 see sth with your own eyes。
keep sb + 形容词表示“使某人保持某种状态”：keeps me busy / calm。

knowledge.quote: But I'd rather they left curious than mournful.
knowledge.explanation: I'd rather + 主语 + 动词过去式表示“我更希望某人（现在/将来）……”，这里的 left 不表示过去，而是虚拟语气。主语相同时才用 I'd rather do。

knowledge.quote: You've been leading walks on this glacier for most of your working life.
knowledge.explanation: 现在完成进行时 have been doing + for 一段时间，强调动作从过去一直持续到现在，而且仍在进行。采访开头问对方的经历时非常自然。

knowledge.quote: you can get a sudden surge through a channel that was ankle-deep an hour earlier
knowledge.explanation: that 引导限定性定语从句修饰 a channel，说明“一小时前还只到脚踝深的”那条水道，用前后对比突出危险来得之快。

speaking: 用 1 分钟介绍一个你去过、这些年明显变了样的地方（景区、海边、老街），说说变化和你的感受，用上 more than anything。
writing: 用 200–250 词写一篇问答式的简短采访，采访一位你想象中的导游或景区工作人员，至少包含一个 I'd rather sb did 结构。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 ..., which ... amounts to the same thing 指出两件看似不同的事其实是一回事。
task.model: It makes it less predictable, which in the mountains amounts to the same thing.

title: 小镇怎样迎接旅游旺季
title_en: How a Small Town Gets Ready for the Summer Rush
summary_zh: 平时安安静静的湖边小镇，一到夏天游客暴增。这篇说明文讲小镇背后看不见的准备：供水、交通、施工时间和居民关系，以及为什么“好的夏天是在冬天建成的”。
body: For most of the year, a small lakeside town runs quietly enough: the buses are half empty, the bakery knows every customer by name, and the single cash machine is rarely out of order. Then summer arrives, and within a few weeks the place can feel as if its population has multiplied. Coping with that seasonal surge is less about grand plans than about dozens of small decisions made months in advance, most of which visitors never notice. Water is often the first concern. Systems designed for the people who live there all year can be inadequate when every holiday flat is full, and in a dry season the needs of tourism and farming may pull in opposite directions. Local councils therefore devise schedules early, deciding which supplies to draw on first and when to ask hotels to cut back, long before the first coach pulls in. Transport is the next headache. Extra buses are useless without drivers, and drivers need somewhere affordable to sleep, which in a popular resort is precisely what is hardest to find. Timing matters as well. Road repairs and the restoration of old buildings are usually scheduled for the off-season, and a project that misses its completion date can leave scaffolding standing through the busiest weeks of the year. In many towns, planners circulate a memo each spring listing every unfinished job, partly so that nothing is quietly forgotten. The most persistent complication, however, is the relationship with residents. Most councils strive to keep a balance, but when parking, noise and rubbish are managed badly, goodwill wears away faster than any harbour wall. The towns that cope best tend to share one habit: they do not neglect the quiet months. Winter is when footpaths are mended, complaints are reviewed and new ideas are tried out on a smaller scale. A good summer, in other words, is mostly built in the rain of the winter before.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
options: Small towns should limit how many tourists arrive each summer
Handling the summer peak depends mostly on planning done in the quieter months
Water shortages are the only serious problem for tourist towns
Residents generally welcome the extra noise and traffic of summer
questions.evidence: A good summer, in other words, is mostly built in the rain of the winter before.

questions.prompt: Why are extra buses not a simple solution?
options: The town's roads are too narrow for large vehicles
There may be no drivers, and drivers struggle to find affordable places to live
Residents object to buses running late at night
Most visitors prefer to arrive by car
questions.evidence: Extra buses are useless without drivers, and drivers need somewhere affordable to sleep

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by "A good summer... is mostly built in the rain of the winter before"?
options: Building work should only happen in summer
Success in the busy season depends on work done in the quiet months
Summers in lakeside towns are usually wet
Rainy winters bring more tourists
questions.evidence: they do not neglect the quiet months

questions.prompt: What does "inadequate" mean in "can be inadequate when every holiday flat is full"?
options: very modern
easy to repair
too expensive
not good enough for what is needed
questions.evidence: can be inadequate when every holiday flat is full

vocabulary.example: Many seaside jobs are seasonal and end when the summer is over.
The school had to devise a new timetable to reduce crowding at lunch.
The organisers will circulate the agenda before the meeting.
Noise is a persistent problem in the old town.
If you neglect small repairs, they soon become big ones.

expressions.note: made months in advance 表示“提前几个月定下的”；订票订房也常说 book in advance。
形容两种需求或力量相互冲突，常用于讨论资源分配。
cut back (on sth) 常指省着用水电、减少开支，比 reduce 更口语。

expressions.meaning: 下一个让人头疼的问题
expressions.note: headache 比喻麻烦事，列举一连串难题时很好用。
常用来说先小范围试点：test the idea on a smaller scale first。
换个说法总结或解释前文，说明文和议论文结尾都很常见。

knowledge.quote: Systems designed for the people who live there all year can be inadequate
knowledge.explanation: 过去分词短语 designed for ... 作后置定语修饰 Systems，表示“为……设计的”，含被动意义；相当于 that were designed for，但更简洁。

knowledge.quote: dozens of small decisions made months in advance, most of which visitors never notice
knowledge.explanation: most of which 引导非限制性定语从句，which 指前面的 decisions。“数量词 + of which/whom”是书面语里把信息连成一句的高级结构。

knowledge.quote: when parking, noise and rubbish are managed badly, goodwill wears away faster than any harbour wall
knowledge.explanation: when 引导状语从句，从句用被动 are managed；主句用 faster than any harbour wall 作比喻，说明居民的好感流失得有多快。

speaking: 用 1 分钟说说你家乡或你熟悉的地方在旅游旺季会遇到什么问题、当地怎么应对，用上 pull in opposite directions 或 the next headache。
writing: 用 200–250 词写一篇说明文，解释某个地方（景区、商场、学校食堂）如何为“高峰期”做准备，至少用两个过去分词作后置定语，结尾用 in other words 总结。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 The ... that ... best tend to share one habit: ... 总结一个你观察到的成功经验。
task.model: The towns that cope best tend to share one habit: they do not neglect the quiet months.

title: 人到中年，出国学画画
title_en: Beginner Again: A Week on a Sketching Course Abroad
summary_zh: 作者报名参加了国外一座山城的一周密集绘画课，结果发现自己是班里年纪最大的学生。这篇随笔讲作者如何放下面子，在重新当“新手”的过程中得到意外的轻松与治愈。
body: I signed up for the course in a moment of optimism, the way some people sign up for marathons. Six days of intensive drawing classes in a hill town, with a room and meals thrown in: it sounded like a holiday with homework. I arrived with a shiny new box of pencils and the confidence of someone who had not been taught anything for twenty years, and discovered within a morning that I was the oldest student in the room by a comfortable margin. The others were art students in their twenties, quick, unembarrassed and alarmingly good at drawing hands. Being a mature beginner, I soon realised, has one real disadvantage and one surprising advantage. The disadvantage is pride. Each evening our teacher, a brisk woman called Elena, pinned our work to the wall for a group critique, and on the first night she remarked, quite kindly, that I drew buildings as though I were filling in a tax form. It stung, mostly because it was true. The advantage is that I no longer mind looking foolish for long. While the younger students seemed to strive for perfection, rubbing out every line that disappointed them, I asked questions constantly, which is, I suspect, how anything is actually learned. By midweek we were sketching outdoors, and I spent a whole afternoon on the green copper dome of the old observatory, the town's most beloved landmark. The woman who ran the café below kept me supplied with delicious almond biscuits and seemed to feel it was her job to entertain me. "My goodness, that's actually good," she said when she saw the finished page, which may have been kindness but felt like a medal. On the last day the group nominated me to give the thank-you speech, presumably on the grounds that I was least likely to cry. I did not quite manage that. Holding my certificate of completion, I realised that the week had been oddly healing: after years of being good at my job, it was a relief to be a beginner again, and to be forgiven for it.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what is the main advantage of being an older beginner?
options: Older students can afford better materials
Caring less about looking foolish makes it easier to ask questions and learn
Teachers tend to give older students gentler feedback
Older students already know how to draw buildings well
questions.evidence: The advantage is that I no longer mind looking foolish for long.

questions.prompt: Why did Elena's comment on the first night sting?
options: Because she said it in a harsh, unkind way
Because the writer knew it was accurate
Because the younger students laughed at it
Because it was about the writer's job rather than the drawing
questions.evidence: It stung, mostly because it was true.

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
options: Why young art students draw hands so well
How being a beginner again on a drawing course proved humbling but rewarding
The best cafés in a hill town
How to become a professional artist
questions.evidence: it was a relief to be a beginner again, and to be forgiven for it

questions.prompt: What does "brisk" mean in "a brisk woman called Elena"?
options: shy
quick and efficient in manner
unfriendly
elderly

vocabulary.example: I took an intensive English course before going abroad.
The teacher gave a short critique of each student’s work.
The nurse was brisk but very kind.
Our team won by a narrow margin.
My classmates nominated me to speak at the graduation dinner.

expressions.note: sign up for a course / class / trip，非常口语化的“报名”。
with sth thrown in 表示套餐里“还包括……”，常见于旅行和购物广告。
原用于比赛、选举，这里幽默地说自己年纪“大出一大截”。
no longer 比 not ... any more 更书面；mind 后接动名词：mind looking foolish。
后接完整句子，书面说明理由；这里带一点自嘲。
it was a relief to do sth 表达压力解除后的轻松，口语、书面都常用。

knowledge.quote: I drew buildings as though I were filling in a tax form
knowledge.explanation: as though / as if 后用虚拟语气（be 动词用 were），表示与事实不符的比喻：并不是真在填税表，只是画得一样死板。

knowledge.quote: Being a mature beginner, I soon realised, has one real disadvantage and one surprising advantage.
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Being a mature beginner 作主语，谓语用单数 has；中间插入 I soon realised，用逗号隔开，读起来像随笔里的自言自语。

knowledge.quote: Holding my certificate of completion, I realised that the week had been oddly healing
knowledge.explanation: 现在分词短语 Holding ... 作伴随状语，逻辑主语就是句子主语 I。用分词开头把动作和感悟放进同一个画面，是随笔的常见写法。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲讲你重新学一样新东西（语言、乐器、运动）的经历：最难的是什么、意外的收获是什么，用上 no longer mind 和 it was a relief to。
writing: 用 200–250 词写一篇个人随笔，回忆一次短期课程或游学经历，至少用一个 as though + were 结构和一个以分词短语开头的句子。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 after years of doing ..., it was a relief to ... 写一次让你重新当“新手”的经历。
task.model: after years of being good at my job, it was a relief to be a beginner again, and to be forgiven for it
